```text
## Pull Requests and Code Review

- **Count:** "Every team member should open exactly 2 pull requests in Sprint 0" (D5).
- **Issue selection:** "The critical rule: implement issues you did not write." Each member implements 2 issues opened by someone else, and "No two team members implement the same issue."
- **Issue assignment:** Teams must "decide who implements which issues before anyone starts coding."
- **Branching:** Use one branch per issue in the team repo, not a fork. Sync with `main` before starting each issue.
- **Base branch:** Select `main` as the base branch when opening the PR.
- **Main is protected:** "Direct pushes to `main` are blocked."
- **Linking:** "The PR must be linked to a GitHub issue (reference it in the description with `Closes #<number>`)."
- **Description:** "The PR description must clearly explain what changed and why, in your own words."
- **Tests:** "Tests must be written or updated for any code changed."
- **Review:** "The PR must be reviewed by at least one other team member before merging (leave a review comment, not just approval)."
- **CI:** "The PR must pass CI if CI is configured in the project." If CI is not configured, note this in the PR description. CI is not required for Sprint 0.
- **Understanding code:** "You must be able to explain every line." Reviewers or the instructor may ask about any part of your change, even after the sprint. Failure to explain code in your own PR results in lost points.
- **Submission:** All PRs live in the project's GitHub repository, and links to merged or reviewed PRs go in the D6 sprint report.
- **Grading (15 points per PR):** Correct implementation without breaking existing tests (5), tests written or updated appropriately (4), a clear PR description (3), and teammate review with comment evidence (3).
- **Minimum bar:** A team with no merged PRs receives 0 for Sprint 0.

## Commits and Branch Naming

- **Branch names:** The guide gives examples using `feat/` for new features and `fix/` for bug fixes, with the issue number and a short description.
- **Commit format:** The example uses a type prefix, a short description, and the issue number in parentheses. Your D3 standards document must define the team's commit convention.
- **Staging:** Add only the files you changed before committing.
- **Testing before commit:** Run tests after making changes and before committing.
- **Cleanup:** Delete branches after they are merged.

## Issues (D2)

- **Minimum:** Each member proposes at least 4 feature ideas as GitHub Issues. More is encouraged.
- **Mix:** Two should be small or medium, and two should be ambitious.
- **Required fields:** Title, Summary, User story, Rough scope, and Source.
- **Labels:** Apply `scope: small`, `scope: medium`, `scope: large`, or `scope: xl`, plus one of `type: feature`, `type: improvement`, or `type: bug`. Use the project's existing labels where available, and create missing ones.
- **Location:** The backlog lives in the GitHub issue tracker, not a separate document.
- **Grading:** Issues are graded on quality, specificity, ambition, completeness of required fields, and labels (20 points).

## AI Usage and Logging (D4)

- **Requirement:** Each member needs at least one agentic AI tool for code-level work.
- **Accounts:** Use your own account. Do not share login credentials or account access with teammates.
- **Log location:** Store logs in `ai-logs/sprint0/<your-github-username>/` in the team repo, following the naming conventions and issue comment format on the AI Log Instructions page.
- **Timing:** Log every agentic session starting from the moment you begin Sprint 0 work.
- **Reporting:** Include a usage summary in D6, and link each member's log folder.
- **Standards document:** D3 must cover which tools the team uses, "what must be logged," review responsibilities for AI-generated code, and "how to flag AI-assisted work in PR descriptions."
- **Project AI files:** Review `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and the AI policy in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, then decide whether to adopt, adapt, or supplement them.

## Testing

- **Baseline:** Run the project's test suite and confirm the baseline passes, as described in `STUDENTS.md`.
- **Evidence:** Include screenshots of the passing test suite in the D6 report.
- **Changed code:** Tests must be written or updated for any code you change.
- **Standards document:** D3 must specify "which types of tests to write for which changes," minimum expectations, and test naming conventions.

## Definition of Done and Standards (D3)

- **Minimum DoD:** The page lists "code reviewed, tests passing, CI green, documentation updated."
- **Project first:** Adopt the project's existing Definition of Done if one exists, and supplement it where it is silent.
- **Other D3 PR topics:** Standards must address PR restrictions, required reviewers, how to write PR descriptions, and merge criteria. The page does not provide a PR template.

## Sprint Report PR Content (D6)

- **Completed PRs table:** Include PR title, issue link, author, reviewer(s), status (merged or open), and a brief description of each change.

## Release Tagging (D7)

- **Pre-tag check:** "Ensure all Sprint 0 PRs are merged (or in a final reviewed state) before tagging."
- **Version:** Use the project's latest version and append `-csci435-s0`. Do not bump the version number. For example, `v2.17.2-csci435-s0`. If no prior release exists, use `v0.1.0-csci435-s0`.
- **Release description:** Write a brief description of what changed in the project.
- **Deadline:** The tag must be pushed by Sep 17, 11:59 PM, and the release linked in D6.
```

```text
## Pull Requests and Branches (D4)

- **PR creation:** "At least one PR per issue must be created, merged, and closed." In most cases, one issue maps to one PR.
- **Linking:** PRs must be "Linked to a GitHub issue (`Closes #<number>` in the description)."
- **Description:** "Description clearly explains _what_ changed, _why_, and _how_ it was tested."
- **Merge timing:** "Merged before the sprint deadline."
- **Branch cleanup:** "Delete the branch after the PR is merged (same as Sprint 0)." Delete both the local and remote branch.
- **Branch naming examples:** `feat/issue-42-export-pdf` (new feature) and `fix/issue-17-date-overflow` (bug fix).
- **Commit message example:** "feat: add PDF export for reports (#42)"
- **Opening the PR:** Use GitHub's "Compare & pull request" banner and select `main` as the base branch.
- **Understanding the code:** "You must be able to explain every line in your PR." Reviewers or the instructor may ask about any part of a change.

## Testing

- "New or updated tests for every behavioral change; test strategy explained in the PR."
- CI "should pass if it is configured for your project." If CI is not working, document manual verification in the PR description.

## Code Review

- Each PR must be reviewed by at least one teammate (not the author) using the rubric.
- The reviewer posts the filled-in rubric as a **comment on the PR**.
- Scores should come from the **initial review pass**, before the author revises. Follow-up revisions may get a brief update note.
- Rubric criteria: Correctness, Test coverage, Code quality, Documentation, AI transparency, and Overall. Each gets a 1–10 score with a 1–2 sentence note.
- Reviewers may also leave line-level comments in GitHub's review interface.
- "Each student must conduct at least one code review per sprint."
- Across the semester, "each student must review code from every teammate at least once."

## Grading of PRs (D4, 36 points total)

Each PR is scored out of 20:

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---|
| Correctly implements D2 acceptance criteria | 6 |
| Tests written or updated; strategy explained in PR | 5 |
| PR description explains what, why, and how tested | 4 |
| CI passes (or manual verification documented) | 3 |
| Reviewed with rubric; reviewer comment posted on PR | 2 |

- Minimum bar: a team with no merged PRs, no sprint report, or no release receives "a **0 for Sprint 1**."
- Extra credit: up to 3 bonus points per PR submitted to the real upstream project and accepted or under active review, at the instructor's discretion.

## Issues (D1, D2)

- Each selected issue needs a single owner, and no issue may be assigned to more than one person.
- Issues must be attached to a milestone named `Sprint 1`.
- Features use a user story, with "Minimum 3" testable acceptance criteria per issue.
- Bug reports need Observed Behavior, Expected Behavior, Steps to Reproduce, and Additional Information.
- Before finalizing a spec, "have at least one teammate read it and leave a comment on the issue" confirming it is clear enough to implement.
- Large or XL issues must be decomposed into smaller sub-issues. If an issue truly needs multiple PRs, split it into sub-issues first.

## Design Decisions (D3)

- Each issue owner documents at least one non-trivial decision, with the decision, at least two alternatives, rationale, and consequences.
- Place these in the issue body, an issue comment, or the PR description. Team-level decisions go in `docs/sprint1/design.md`.

## AI Usage and Logging (D5)

- **Scope:** Every agentic session related to Sprint 1 work must be logged.
- **Location and naming:** Store logs in `ai-logs/sprint1/<github-username>/` as `YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`.
- **Content:** Logs must capture "full session metadata: timestamps, prompts, and AI responses."
- **Timing:** "Do not summarize or reconstruct your AI usage after the fact. Logs must be captured during the session."
- **Accepted formats:** `.md` (preferred), `.txt`, or `.json`. "Do not submit `.html`, `.docx`, or `.pdf` log files, or links to private chats."
- **Where to link:** References go in an **issue comment**, not the PR description or a PR comment. "Logs not linked to an issue comment will not receive credit."
- **Per contributor:** "Each contributor (implementor, code reviewer, estimator) posts their own comment on the issue."
- **No AI used:** Post a note in an issue comment, and the log folder must still exist.

## Sprint Report (D6)

- Per-PR table columns: PR link, author, reviewer(s), and status, plus the issue title, owner, and a brief description of changes.
- Per-member AI usage: tools used, sessions logged, and a link to the AI log folder.
- Test strategy: the kinds of tests written and any changes that could not be tested automatically, with reasons.

## Release (D7)

- "Ensure all Sprint 1 PRs are merged before tagging."
- "Use the same base version from Sprint 0 (no version bump)."
- Tag with the `-csci435-s1` suffix, e.g., `v2.17.2-csci435-s1`.
- Write a release description listing features added, bugs fixed, or improvements made this sprint.
- Tag and GitHub release are due by Oct 8, 11:59 PM.

The page does not define a PR template or a formal commit message standard beyond the examples above.
```

```text
## Pull Requests and Code Review

- **Self-review ban:** "A student cannot approve or merge their own PR." Reviewers must leave substantive comments, not just approve.
- **Review turnaround:** Notify your reviewer in your team's Zulip channel (or by email) when a PR is ready. Aim to respond within 24 hours.
- **Workflow:** Follows Sprint 1's PR workflow, which the Sprint 2 page does not restate.
- **PR description:** Must explain what changed, why, and how it was tested, and must include the Tech Debt section (see below).
- **Tech Debt section (required in every PR):** Two fields, "Introduced" and "Encountered." Both are required. "None." is an accepted answer. PRs missing the section lose points.
- **Code review rubric:** Reviewer must post the rubric as a comment on each PR.
- **Merged PRs:** All PRs must be merged by the deadline.
- **Minimum bar:** A team with no merged PRs, no sprint report, or no release receives 0 for Sprint 2.
- **Per-PR grading (20 points):**
  - Implements the D2 acceptance criteria (6)
  - Tests written or updated, with the test strategy explained in the PR (5)
  - Description covers what, why, and how tested, plus Tech Debt section (4)
  - CI passes, or manual verification is documented (3)
  - Reviewed with the rubric and a reviewer comment posted (2)
- **Extra credit:** Up to 3 bonus points per PR submitted to the real upstream project and accepted or under active review, at the instructor's discretion.

## Commits and Branches

The Sprint 2 page does not state any commit or branch requirements.

## Issues

- **Sprint 1 carryovers:** Unfinished Sprint 1 issues take priority and go into the Sprint 2 backlog before new work. If you drop one, document the reason on the issue. Acceptable reasons are that the issue was closed, is invalid after later changes, or is no longer relevant.
- **Scope minimums:**
  - CSCI 435: at least 2 medium issues (or equivalent story points).
  - CSCI 535: at least 2 medium issues plus 1 additional small issue.
- **Issue creation:** If the backlog is short, write new issues with a user story, acceptance criteria, and an estimate.
- **Milestone:** Create a "Sprint 2" milestone in GitHub and attach all selected issues.
- **Specs (D2):** Written and peer-reviewed before coding starts. Follows user story format and INVEST criteria.
- **Design decisions (D3):** Each decision must name at least two concrete alternatives and explain the choice. Issue bodies must be updated with user stories, acceptance criteria, and design decisions.

## AI Usage and Logging

- **Completeness:** Logs must contain the full session, including the prompts you wrote and the AI output. Summaries do not count, and output without its prompts is incomplete.
- **Linking:** Every issue or PR involving AI use needs a comment linking directly to the specific log file. A link to a folder or to a different issue or PR does not count. Use the template from the AI Log Instructions page.
- **Format:** SpecStory is strongly recommended. Screenshots are not logs.
- **Storage:** `ai-logs/sprint2/<github-username>/`
- **File naming:** `YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`
- **Report:** Include an AI log summary in the sprint report (D8).
- **Setup:** Verify your AI log setup before starting new agentic sessions. Contact the instructors promptly if you have logging problems.
- **Diagrams (D6):** Describe any AI use in creating or checking the diagrams, including what you verified and corrected, or write "N/A."

## Testing

- Tests must be written or updated appropriately, and the PR must explain the test strategy (5 points per PR).
- CI must pass, or manual verification must be documented (3 points per PR).

## Release Notes and Tagging (D9)

- **Tag format:** Use the Sprint 1 version with the `-csci435-s2` suffix. Example: `v2.17.2-csci435-s1` becomes `v2.17.2-csci435-s2`.
- **Release description:** Must summarize the sprint's changes.
- **Deadline:** Tag pushed and GitHub release created by Oct 29, 11:59 PM.
- **Submission:** Link the GitHub release in the sprint report (D8).

## Key Deadlines

- Mid-sprint check-in (D7): Oct 22, 11:59 PM
- All other deliverables, including the tag and reflection survey: Oct 29, 11:59 PM
```

```text
## Description

<!-- What does this PR do? Why is it needed? Please give context on the "why?": why do we need this change? What problem is it solving for you?-->

<!-- If AI tools wrote a significant part of this change, please disclose it here and name the tool you used. See https://actualbudget.org/docs/contributing/ai-usage-policy -->

This PR adds a percentage-based version of the user's change in net worth and displays it in the Net Worth Report and Net Worth Widget. It added the totalChangePercent attribute to the net worth spreadsheet (0 when there is no change, null when starting net worth is 0) and display it next to the dollar change in the net worth report and dashboard widget, using -- for the null case. This helps users not only see the exact amount their net worth has changed but how significant that change is in a percentage.
```

```text
Add percentage of YTD change in net worth under "reports" | state: open | assignees: ['RaccoonSwarm'] | milestone: None | labels: ['scope: medium']
## Summary

Users viewing the Net Worth report already have a "Yearly" interval and a built-in year-to-date time-frame mode (`TimeFrame['mode']` in `packages/loot-core/src/types/models/dashboard.ts` already includes `'yearToDate'`), and the net-worth spreadsheet (`net-worth-spreadsheet.ts`) already computes a `totalChange` (end balance minus start balance) for whatever range is selected — it also already handles the case where an account's earliest transaction falls after the range start, adjusting the lookback so a new account doesn't produce a misleading empty gap. What's missing is a percentage-based version of that change: today `totalChange` is only ever shown as a raw dollar amount via the existing `Change` component, with no percentage/directional badge next to it.

## User Story

As a user tracking my long-term financial health, I want to see a YTD percentage change next to my net worth on the reports page so that I can instantly gauge my financial growth over the current year at a glance.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The Net Worth report page (and/or its dashboard card — see Open Question #1) shows a percentage-change value alongside the existing dollar `Change` amount.
2. The percentage is computed as `(endNetWorth - startNetWorth) / abs(startNetWorth) * 100`, using the same start/end balances the existing `totalChange` calculation already derives internally in `net-worth-spreadsheet.ts` — no new query/engine logic is required; `startNetWorth` just needs to be added to what `recalculate()` returns.
3. The percentage badge uses the same directional color convention as the existing `Change` component (positive / negative / neutral).
4. If the starting balance is exactly $0 (e.g. a brand-new budget with no prior net worth), the percentage is not rendered as `Infinity` or `NaN` — show a fallback (e.g. "N/A", or hide the percentage) instead.
5. Formatting matches the currency/decimal and percentage conventions used elsewhere in Actual.

## Out of Scope

- A percentage-change indicator for time ranges other than YTD (e.g. last month, last year, custom range) — this issue is scoped to the YTD case only.
- Any change to how the underlying net worth balance itself is calculated — this only adds a percentage *view* of numbers already computed.
- A historical chart of percentage change over time — this is a single point-in-time indicator, not a new graph.

## Open Questions

1. Should this live on the full Net Worth report page, the condensed Net Worth dashboard card, or both? The dollar `Change` component is currently only used on the full report page (`NetWorth.tsx`) — confirm whether the card view needs it too.
2. For an account created mid-year, the existing spreadsheet logic already shifts the lookback start date to that account's earliest transaction rather than Jan 1, so its "starting balance" isn't really a Jan-1 balance. Is a percentage computed against that adjusted starting balance still meaningful, or should such accounts be excluded from the percentage calculation while still counting toward the dollar total?
3. Should the percentage always reflect calendar YTD (Jan 1 to today) regardless of whatever interval/time-frame the user has selected in the report's own controls, or should it track whatever range is currently selected and only be labeled "YTD" when that range happens to be the year-to-date one?

## Rough Scope

Medium — The original "Large" estimate assumed new engine-level query logic was needed, but the YTD time-frame mode and the mid-year-account lookback handling already exist in `net-worth-spreadsheet.ts`, and the starting balance needed for a percentage is already computed internally (just not currently returned). The remaining work is exposing that value, adding a percentage-formatting UI element following the existing `Change` component's pattern, and resolving Open Questions #1–#3 about exactly where and how it should apply — mostly UI wiring and edge-case handling rather than new financial-engine work.

## Source

Community feature request / GitHub issue discussion.
```

```text
import React from 'react';
import type { CSSProperties } from 'react';

import { Block } from '@actual-app/components/block';
import { styles } from '@actual-app/components/styles';
import { theme } from '@actual-app/components/theme';

import { FinancialText } from '#components/FinancialText';
import { useFormat } from '#hooks/useFormat';

export function Change({
  amount,
  percent,
  style,
}: {
  amount: number;
  // Omit to hide the percentage; null renders a placeholder
  percent?: number | null;
  style?: CSSProperties;
}) {
  const format = useFormat();

  let percentText = '';
  if (percent === null) {
    percentText = ' (--)';
  } else if (percent !== undefined) {
    percentText = ` (${percent > 0 ? '+' : ''}${percent.toFixed(1)}%)`;
  }

  return (
    <FinancialText
      as={Block}
      style={{
        ...styles.smallText,
        color:
          amount === 0
            ? theme.reportsNumberNeutral
            : amount < 0
              ? theme.reportsNumberNegative
              : theme.reportsNumberPositive,
        ...style,
      }}
    >
      {format(amount, 'financial-with-sign')}
      {percentText}
    </FinancialText>
  );
}
```

```text
This PR adds a percentage-based version of the user's change in net worth and displays it in the Net Worth Report and Net Worth Widget. It added the totalChangePercent attribute to the net worth spreadsheet (0 when there is no change, null when starting net worth is 0) and display it next to the dollar change in the net worth report and dashboard widget, using -- for the null case. This helps users not only see the exact amount their net worth has changed but how significant that change is in a percentage.
```

````text
# Running VRTs (Visual Regression Tests) in actualbudget/actual
VRTs are ordinary Playwright e2e tests in `packages/desktop-client/e2e/*.test.ts` that call:
```ts
await expect(target).toMatchThemeScreenshots();
```
`toMatchThemeScreenshots()` is a custom matcher defined in
`packages/desktop-client/e2e/fixtures.ts`. `target` is a `Page` or a `Locator` —
**prefer a tight locator** (e.g. a popover or panel) over the whole page to
reduce noise from charts and data.
## Key mechanics
- **No-op without `VRT=true`.** In a plain e2e run the matcher passes
  immediately, so `yarn workspace @actual-app/web run playwright test <file> -g "<name>"`
  verifies the interaction flow cheaply without needing snapshots — always do
  this first.
- **With `VRT=true`, each call captures three themes** (`auto` i.e. light,
  `dark`, `midnight`), producing numbered snapshots:
  `<file>.test.ts-snapshots/<Describe>-<test-name>-N-chromium-linux.png`.
  One test with 2 assertions → 6 PNGs.
- **Masking:** elements with `data-vrt-mask="true"` are masked out of
````

# Committing Changes in actualbudget/actual

Before creating any git commit or pull request in this repo, read:

**`.github/agents/pr-and-commit-rules.md`**

It is the authoritative source for the rules you must apply yourself: the `[AI]` PR-title prefix and leaving the PR template blank (and the Chinese exception). The mechanical commit/git rules are enforced by tooling and aren't restated there. Read it on every commit/PR session so any updates are picked up automatically.

## The one rule worth restating

Every commit message and every pull request title MUST begin with `[AI]`. Commit messages are checked by the git-guard hook (a missing prefix is blocked before the commit lands), so the one that needs _your_ attention is the PR title — nothing checks it for you, and the cost of forgetting it is high since the PR has to be renamed by hand. Examples:

- `[AI] Fix type error in account validation` — correct
- `Fix type error in account validation` — wrong, missing prefix

The PR-template rule and the rest live in the rules file. Read it before each commit/PR rather than relying on this skill's summary, because the rules file evolves and this skill deliberately does not restate it.

## Why this matters

Maintainers triage AI-authored contributions separately, and the `[AI]` prefix is what makes that triage fast — it also drives the automatic `"AI generated"` PR label, so getting the prefix right is the one action that gates the whole triage path. Without it the PR looks like a normal human contribution and the wrong review process gets applied. The "do not fill in the PR template" rule exists because the human is the one who actually tested the change and can write the Description / Testing / Checklist sections honestly — an AI-filled template misrepresents who did what.

The rules file is short. Read it.
